title: Status Codes and Response Metadata
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of status codes and response metadata in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to setting status codes.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers status codes and response metadata within responses, errors, and validation. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use status codes and response metadata to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is clear input/output contracts, field validation, serialization and safe defaults.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Status Codes and Response Metadata matters because it is part of responses, errors, and validation. In practice, focus on clear input/output contracts, field validation, serialization and safe defaults. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: Setting status codes
items.text: Use setting status codes to make behavior observable and repeatable. Specify one normal case, one invalid or missing-input case, and the expected status or diagnostic. A passing happy path alone is not enough evidence.

items.title: Using 201 Created
items.text: Use using 201 created as a design decision rather than a keyword to memorize. State the input and expected result, identify the boundary conditions, and connect the concept to the surrounding FastAPI request lifecycle.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to cover “Setting status codes”. Write down the expected success result and one invalid, missing, duplicate, timeout or permission-boundary case that matters for this topic.

task: Create a small reviewable artifact for “Status Codes and Response Metadata”: explain its goal, cover the listed subtopics, show an example with expected result, then include one edge case and how you would verify it.
hints: Start with “Setting status codes” and state the required inputs, output and assumptions.
Change one thing at a time; check the official reference and capture the actual response/error instead of guessing.
Include a negative/edge-case check and document which behavior remains untested.
expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Status Codes and Response Metadata, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.

summary: Status Codes and Response Metadata belongs to the broader goal of clear input/output contracts, field validation, serialization and safe defaults.
Use the source subtopics as the completeness checklist and verify expected results rather than relying on intuition.
Examples in this course are illustrative until technically reviewed and executed on a supported local environment.
